title: NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops go on sale with 128GB unified memory for 24/7 local agents
summary: NVIDIA, Asus, Dell, and MSI have started selling RTX Spark compact desktops. The pitch isn't a faster workstation; it's an always-on computer that runs agents locally.
ai_summary: NVIDIA, Asus, Dell, and MSI have put RTX Spark compact desktops on sale, with Acer, Gigabyte, HP, and Microsoft Surface models to follow. The selling point isn't raw speed: it's a computer that stays on so agents can work locally. With up to 128GB of unified memory, a large model can fit entirely on the machine, everyday tasks run locally, and only complex reasoning goes to the cloud. It isn't cheap: MSI's 64GB model costs $4,699 and the 128GB model $7,999. It's for individual developers and small teams who want to keep data on-site and run agents for long stretches; if you just do occasional Q&A, cloud services are the better deal.
brief: RTX Spark compact desktops from Asus, Dell, and MSI are available now; Acer, Gigabyte, HP, and Microsoft Surface models will follow.
Up to 128GB of unified memory: at low precision, a 120-billion-parameter model can fit entirely on the machine.
Hermes Agent adds Switchyard: everyday tasks go to a local model, and only complex reasoning calls the cloud.

sections.h: What kind of machine is this

blocks.p: RTX Spark is NVIDIA's Windows PC platform: its own Grace CPU (Arm-based) and Blackwell GPU sit on the same chip, and the CPU and GPU share a single pool of memory. That chip first appeared in laptops; now it's going into compact desktops.
The first models on sale come from Asus, Dell, and MSI; Acer, Gigabyte, HP, and the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box will follow.

blocks.p: NVIDIA gives three uses: running 120-billion-parameter large models locally, rendering 3D scenes larger than 90GB in real time, and editing 4:2:2 video in real time.

sections.h: Why you need an always-on computer

blocks.p: Agents and scheduled tasks keep working when you're away. Batch image generation, running tests, and organizing files can continue after you leave your computer. A laptop gets closed and carried around, so it's a poor fit for this background work; a compact desktop that stays plugged in fills the gap.

blocks.p: Running this locally has two direct benefits: files processed by a local model never leave the machine, and these tasks aren't billed by the token like cloud API calls.

sections.h: How large a model can 128GB hold?

blocks.p: In a typical desktop, system memory and graphics memory are separate, and a model has to fit into GPU memory to run fast. In RTX Spark, the CPU and GPU share one pool of memory, up to 128GB, so a model can be loaded in its entirety.

The math is simple: model size ≈ number of parameters × bytes per parameter. FP16 takes 2 bytes per parameter, FP8 takes 1 byte, and FP4 takes half a byte. For 120 billion parameters, that's about 240GB, 120GB, and 60GB respectively.

blocks.p: So “running a 120-billion-parameter model locally” assumes low precision such as FP4. Fitting doesn't mean fast: generation speed depends mainly on memory bandwidth, and MSI lists 273GB/s on its site.

sections.h: Everyday work stays local; hard problems go to the cloud

blocks.p: For development, RTX Spark supports CUDA, so you can build agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune models with Unsloth.

Hermes Agent now adds NVIDIA Switchyard: as each task arrives, it automatically decides whether to send it to a local or cloud model. Everyday tasks run on the machine; only tasks that need advanced reasoning call the cloud, so cloud costs go toward hard problems alone.

sections.h: Adobe apps get native Arm versions

blocks.p: RTX Spark's CPU uses the Arm architecture, while most Windows software is written for x86; without a native version, it runs through an emulation layer and takes a speed hit. Adobe has now released several native Windows on Arm versions with RTX acceleration.

fig.title: Native apps skip the translation layer, so they're faster
fig.subtitle: Illustrative
fig.note: The “up to 30% faster” figure comes from NVIDIA's blog; actual gains vary by task.

list: Premiere: Enhance Speech, object masks, scene edit detection, and Auto Reframe are accelerated by TensorRT-RTX; it adds support for Canon RAW, RED RAW, ARRI RAW, ProRes RAW, and more; everyday H.264 delivery is over 50% faster.
Photoshop: the Remove tool is accelerated by TensorRT-RTX, and Camera Raw runs natively.
Substance 3D Painter 12.2: native Arm version now in public beta.
Illustrator and InDesign: native Arm versions are out, and Illustrator is up to 30% faster than the emulated version.

sections.h: Blender 5.3: no more waiting for preview noise to clear

blocks.p: Blender's Cycles renderer uses ray tracing to compute the image: viewport previews start out full of noise, need many samples to clean up, and reset whenever you move the camera. Blender 5.3 brings DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, using AI to fill in an image that's close to final.

blocks.p: Requirements: Blender 5.3, plus the latest Game Ready or Studio driver.

So far, only MSI has public pricing. According to TweakTown, citing MSI's US site, the EdgeMesa N AI+ comes in two configurations: 64GB of memory plus 1TB of storage for $4,699, and 128GB of memory plus 4TB of storage for $7,999. The memory is soldered to the motherboard, so it can't be upgraded later.

Compare that with NVIDIA's own Linux compact desktop on the same chip, DGX Spark: in February the 128GB model went from $3,999 to $4,699, then rose again to $6,950 in October, when a $4,999 64GB version also appeared.

fig.title: The 64GB tier is cheaper; the 128GB tier is actually more expensive
fig.subtitle: USD, US retail prices
fig.note: The MSI 64GB model is $300 cheaper than the 64GB DGX Spark; the 128GB model costs $1,049 more.

blocks.p: The value of this machine is having up to 128GB of unified memory for large models in a Windows PC that also runs the usual Adobe, Blender, and CUDA toolchain. An agent can stay running, and work is automatically split between local and cloud.
The trade-offs are just as clear: the 128GB version costs nearly $8,000, memory is not upgradeable, and 1 petaflop is a peak figure, not everyday speed.

list: If you mostly do occasional Q&A, cloud services are simpler.
If you have lots of files you don't want to upload, or batch jobs that can run overnight, it's worth considering.
If your monthly cloud token bill is already significant, calculate how much local offloading could save.
